---
applyTo: "app/services/**/*.rb,app/forms/**/*.rb,app/controllers/**/*.rb,app/jobs/**/*.rb"
---

# Services

- Put service objects in `app/services/`, e.g. `NewsletterClient` in `app/services/newsletter_client.rb`.
- You MUST NOT give a service object a `call` method. Name each public method after what it does, e.g. `NewsletterClient#create_newsletter` and `NewsletterClient#deliver`.
- Make one request to the other service in each public service method. When one request needs the reply to another, link them in an action: call the first method, and pass the reply on to the second, e.g. `Posts::SendNewsletter` calls `NewsletterClient#create_public_newsletter`, saves `newsletter.id` on the post, then enqueues `NotifySubscribersJob`, which calls `NewsletterClient#deliver`. You SHOULD NOT chain requests inside a service method, e.g. `NewsletterClient#create_and_deliver`.
- A request that only reads, whose reply the app never keeps or uses, and that only serves another request, MAY stay in the service, e.g. fetching an access token, or looking up the other service's own ID for one of yours. A request that changes something in the other service goes through an action, even when the app doesn't keep its reply, e.g. reserving a slot before booking it. Make it in a private method, e.g. `NewsletterClient#find_list_id("Weekly digest")` in `create_public_newsletter`. When the app saves its reply, link the requests in an action instead.
- Call a service for another system from an action, not from a form or controller, e.g. `NewsletterClient.new.create_newsletter(title: post.title, body: post.body)` in `Posts::SendNewsletter#call`. Forms, controllers and jobs call the action. A form or controller MAY call a service directly only to read a value when nothing changes, e.g. `NewsletterClient.new.fetch_stats(post.newsletter_id)` in a controller. A controller reads the value before the view renders, following the controllers instructions. A job MAY call a service directly only when it is the only place that does the task, e.g. `NewsletterClient.new.deliver(post.newsletter_id)` in `NotifySubscribersJob`. Move the call into an action when a second caller needs it.
- Take only the values the caller decides, as keyword arguments, and fill in the rest in the service, e.g. from its settings, its options, a lookup or a fixed value. Two methods MAY send to the same endpoint with different values filled in, e.g. `NewsletterClient#create_public_newsletter(title:, body:)` and `NewsletterClient#create_private_newsletter(title:, body:)`, each with its own `visibility`. Read the values from the records in the caller, e.g. `NewsletterClient.new.create_public_newsletter(title: post.title, body: post.body)` in `Posts::SendPublicNewsletter#call`.
- You SHOULD NOT pass a record to a service method that makes a request, e.g. `create_public_newsletter(post)`.
- You MUST NOT make the caller pass a value the service can fill in itself, e.g. the API key, or the ID of the "Weekly digest" list.
- Build a service's request body in the service, as a hash. When it takes more than a line, build it in a private method on the service named after what it builds, e.g. `NewsletterClient#newsletter_body(title:, body:, visibility:)`, not in a class in `app/models/`. A class the app uses for its own work stays with the rest of the app's code, e.g. in `app/models/` or `app/serializers/`. You MUST NOT make the caller build the body, e.g. a hash with the other service's field names.
- When a method takes more values than keyword arguments can carry, the service MAY define a `Data` object for the request at its top, e.g. `CreateNewsletterRequest = Data.define(:title, :body, :preheader, :send_at, :reply_to, :track_opens, :track_clicks)` in `NewsletterClient`. Use keyword arguments otherwise. Name the request after the operation it's for, e.g. `CreateNewsletterRequest`, and share it between methods that do the same operation with different values filled in, e.g. `create_public_newsletter(request)` and `create_private_newsletter(request)`. Give an operation that takes other fields its own request, e.g. `UpdateNewsletterRequest`. You MUST NOT use a `Struct` for it.
- Build a service's request object in the caller, e.g. `NewsletterClient::CreateNewsletterRequest.new(title: post.title, body: post.body, **settings)` in `Posts::SendPublicNewsletter#call`. You MUST NOT make the caller build a request for the gem the service calls, e.g. a request class the gem defines.
- Return a service's reply as an object the caller reads by its fields, e.g. `response.id`. You SHOULD NOT return a hash. A service MAY define a `Data` object for a reply at its top, named after what it holds, e.g. `Newsletter = Data.define(:id, :status)` in `NewsletterClient`. You MUST NOT use a `Struct` for it.
- You SHOULD NOT return the reply of a gem the service calls, e.g. the `Aws::S3::Types::PutObjectOutput` from `Aws::S3::Client#put_object`. Build the service's own reply from it, or return the one value the caller needs.
- You MUST NOT name a service's reply class outside the service, e.g. `NewsletterClient::Newsletter` in an action. Read its fields instead.
- When another service returns results a page at a time, read one page in each service method. Take the cursor as a keyword argument and return it with the page, e.g. `NewsletterClient#list_newsletters(cursor: nil)` returning `newsletters` and `next_cursor`. Let the caller read the next page, e.g. `SyncNewslettersJob.perform_later(page.next_cursor)` in `SyncNewslettersJob#perform`. You SHOULD NOT read every page in the service.
- Define a service's request and reply classes at its top. When they crowd out its methods, the service MAY move each one into its own file in a folder named after the service, e.g. `NewsletterClient::CreateNewsletterRequest` in `app/services/newsletter_client/create_newsletter_request.rb`. You MUST NOT move a service's request or reply classes into `app/models/`.
- Read a service's settings from a `Rails.application.config.x` namespace named after the service, e.g. `config.x.newsletter_client.api_key`. Set the values in one place, e.g. `config/application.rb`, from credentials or `ENV`. You MUST NOT read `Rails.application.credentials` or `ENV` in a service, and you MUST NOT put a setting straight on `config.x`, e.g. `config.x.newsletter_client_api_key`.
- Take each setting as a keyword argument to `initialize`, with the setting as its default, e.g. `def initialize(api_key: Rails.application.config.x.newsletter_client.api_key!)`. Read required settings with a bang, e.g. `api_key!`, so a missing or blank value raises a `KeyError`. You MUST NOT pass the settings from app code, e.g. `NewsletterClient.new`, not `NewsletterClient.new(api_key: ...)`. Only specs pass them, e.g. `described_class.new(api_key: "test-key")`.
- Set the options a service gives its client or library inside the service, in a constant or a private method, e.g. `faraday.request :json` in `NewsletterClient#connection`, or `Commonmarker.to_html(markdown, options: OPTIONS)` in `MarkdownRenderer#render_html`. Options are values no caller needs to send, so callers pass only what changes with each call. Keep them out of `config.x`, because they are the same in every environment.
- Give every service a timeout, read from its `config.x` namespace like its other settings, e.g. `timeout_seconds: Rails.application.config.x.newsletter_client.timeout_seconds!`, and pass it to the HTTP library, e.g. `Faraday.new(url: @base_url, request: { timeout: @timeout_seconds })`. When the service keeps a connection pool, pass its timeouts to `pool_for`, not to `initialize`, e.g. `timeout_seconds: Rails.application.config.x.newsletter_client.timeout_seconds!` on `NewsletterClient.pool_for`. A service MAY take more than one timeout when one step needs its own limit, e.g. `open_timeout_seconds` and `read_timeout_seconds`. Name each after what it limits, ending with its unit. Set the timeouts below the app's request timeout, e.g. `config.x.newsletter_client.timeout_seconds = 10` under rack-timeout's `service_timeout: 15`, so a request that calls the service gets the service's own error. When an action makes more than one request, keep their timeouts together below the limit.
- When the app can run without a service, give the service a `configured?` class method that checks its required settings without the bang, e.g. `config.api_key.present? && config.base_url.present?` on `Rails.application.config.x.newsletter_client`. Check it before building the service in code that can skip the work, e.g. `return unless NewsletterClient.configured?` in `NotifySubscribersJob#perform`. You MUST NOT add a separate `enabled` setting, and you MUST NOT rescue `KeyError` to find out whether a service is set up.
- When a service's settings are saved on a record, build it with a class method on the service that passes the record's settings to `new`, named `for` or `for_<source>`, e.g. `for_integration`. For example, `def self.for(integration) = new(api_key: integration.api_key, base_url: integration.base_url)` on `NewsletterClient`. Make those settings required keywords with no default, and leave app-wide settings to their `config.x` defaults, e.g. `api_path: Rails.application.config.x.newsletter_client.api_path!`. You MUST NOT add a method to the record that builds the service, e.g. `integration.client`.
- When a service keeps connections open to another service, borrow them from a `ConnectionPool` kept on the service in a private `Concurrent::Map` constant and keyed on the connection settings, e.g. `POOLS.compute_if_absent({ base_url: })` in `NewsletterClient.pool_for(base_url:)`. Take the pool as a required first argument to `initialize`, e.g. `def initialize(pool, api_key:)`, and borrow from it in each method, e.g. `pool.with { |connection| ... }`. Build the service with a class method that finds the pool: `NewsletterClient.default` when every setting comes from `config.x`, e.g. `new(pool_for(base_url: Rails.application.config.x.newsletter_client.base_url!), api_key: Rails.application.config.x.newsletter_client.api_key!)`, or `NewsletterClient.for(integration)` (or `for_integration`) when the settings come from a record, e.g. `new(pool_for(base_url: integration.base_url), api_key: integration.api_key)`. Pass connection settings only to `pool_for`, and keep `pool_for` private. You MUST NOT pass a pool to `new` from outside the service. Only specs and the service's own class methods pass one. You MUST NOT let a pooled connection carry one set of credentials to a service built with another. Send credentials with each request, e.g. an `Authorization` header, or include them in the pool's key. See https://bmorrall.github.io/happy_rails/patterns/connection-pools/.
- Write a service only to talk to another system, e.g. `NewsletterClient` for the newsletter service's HTTP API or `PostBackupBucket` around `Aws::S3::Client`, or to wrap a library the app uses for its own work, e.g. `MarkdownRenderer` around Commonmarker or `PostPdf` around Prawn. Keep a calculation on a record in its model, e.g. a post's word count, and put a task that changes data in an action.
- Apply the rules for requests, replies, pages, timeouts and gateways only to services for other systems. A service for the app's own work follows the rules for method names, configuration and errors.
- You MUST NOT save records in a service. Return the result, and save it in the action that called the service, e.g. `post.update!(newsletter_id: newsletter.id)` in `Posts::SendNewsletter#call`.
- Give each service its own errors: an `Error < StandardError` class inside the service, e.g. `NewsletterClient::Error`. Rescue the HTTP library's errors in the service and raise the service's error, e.g. `rescue Faraday::Error => e` then `raise Error.new(e.message, ...)`. You MUST NOT let a library's error escape a service.
- A service MAY raise a subclass of its `Error` for a failure a caller handles on its own. Add one only when a caller needs it, e.g. `rescue Faraday::TimeoutError => e` then `raise TimeoutError.new(e.message, ...)`. Rescue the library's specific errors before its base error, e.g. before `rescue Faraday::Error`.
- Define a service's error classes in the service's file, e.g. `NewsletterClient::Error` and `NewsletterClient::TimeoutError` in `app/services/newsletter_client.rb`, even when its request and reply classes have their own files.
- Name a service's error subclass after its failure, e.g. `UnprocessableError` when the other service rejects the request, e.g. `Faraday::UnprocessableEntityError`; `TimeoutError` when the request times out, e.g. `Faraday::TimeoutError`; `UnavailableError` when the other service can't be reached or is down, e.g. `Faraday::ConnectionFailed` or a 503 reply; `RateLimitedError` when it says the app sent too many requests, e.g. `Faraday::TooManyRequestsError`; `UnauthorizedError` when it refuses the credentials, e.g. `Faraday::UnauthorizedError` or `Faraday::ForbiddenError`; `NotFoundError` when it doesn't have the resource, e.g. `Faraday::ResourceNotFound`.
- Give a `RateLimitedError` the reply's `Retry-After` value, e.g. `retry_after:` on `NewsletterClient::RateLimitedError`.
- Give a service's error the details of the failed call as keywords, e.g. `http_method:`, `url:`, `status:` and `body:` on `NewsletterClient::Error`.
- A service SHOULD call the other system through its gem when it has one, e.g. `Aws::S3::Client` in `PostBackupBucket`. When the other system has no gem, make the HTTP calls in the service, e.g. with Faraday in `NewsletterClient`.
- You SHOULD NOT write a gateway, your own client for the whole API in `lib/`, unless the API has no gem, and either several services share it or its HTTP code has outgrown the service. See https://bmorrall.github.io/happy_rails/patterns/apis-without-a-gem/.
